growth_story.headline: Mongolia's growth follows its mines: a post-Soviet collapse, a mining boom, a bust after 2015, then a copper-led record high in 2025.
growth_story.arc: Income per person shrank by 2.1 percent a year in 1990–1997, when Soviet aid ended just as Mongolia began moving to a market economy, and it fell 11.5 percent in 1991 alone. Growth came back at 3.7 percent a year in 1998–2005, led at first by herding and crops, and it sped up from 2003. In 2006–2014 it averaged 7.2 percent, as foreign money poured into mining, and it reached 15.3 percent in 2011. Since 2015 it has averaged 2.3 percent. Falling commodity prices and rising public debt brought growth close to zero in 2015 and 2016, and the pandemic, with China's border restrictions, brought a fall of 6.3 percent in 2020. A mining boom in 2023–24 and a copper surge in 2025 lifted income per person to its highest level yet in 2025, but the last decade's average of 2.5 percent is still far below the 6.5 of the decade before.

threads.title: Losing Soviet aid
threads.text: When Soviet support ended, Mongolia lost aid worth a large share of its economy. Income per person hit bottom in 1993. The recovery that followed came from market reforms that made the economy more efficient, with herding and crops leading.

threads.title: Foreign money builds mines
threads.text: From the mid-2000s, foreign investment in mining drove the fastest growth on record, with income per person up 15.3 percent in 2011. The boom ran through 2014, when growth was still 5.6 percent.

threads.title: Commodity bust and debt
threads.text: Commodity prices fell from 2011, hurting the balance of payments and the budget, and earlier easy policy had pushed up public debt. Income per person grew just 0.2 percent in 2015 and fell 0.5 percent in 2016, and an IMF-backed program followed in 2017.

threads.title: Pandemic and border closures
threads.text: Income per person fell 6.3 percent in 2020 and stayed flat in 2021. China's pandemic rules held back exports, and the fall in mining output eased only as limits on cross-border trade were relaxed in 2022.

threads.title: From coal to copper
threads.text: Mongolia relies on a few mined goods such as coal and copper, and the sources link this to repeated booms and busts. Mining boomed in 2023–24, then coal weakened and a surge in copper output took over as the main driver.

since_last_year.text: Coal exports fell sharply in the first half of 2025, but growth held up: copper output jumped and farming bounced back after two years of climate-related losses. Income per person grew 5.5 percent in 2025 and reached its highest level yet.

growth_story.tension: The IMF found that total output was back to its pre-transition level by 2000–01, but income per person did not pass its 1990 level until 2004, which points to population growth. The data also call 2015–2025 a slow era at 2.3 percent a year, while the sources describe boom years in 2023–2025. Most of the drag in that era comes from 2015–2016 and 2020–2021.
